episode_thesis: The panel explains 2024 trend following as a slow-and-large-market year: only equities and a few commodities trended, policy-expectation noise punished fast and medium speeds, and August's V-shaped shock hurt medium-speed models. Dispersion among managers came from speed, universe, purity and de-risking, while vol selling and structured products pinned the index; the panel debated crowding, whether illiquid markets trend more, market efficiency and AI.

speakers.name: Katy Kaminski
speakers.role: Quant researcher, trend following (CTA style factors)

worldview_premises.premise: Trend performance is set by which trends exist and at which speed; in a year with one clear large-market trend, slow signals win and fast ones lose.
worldview_premises.support: Annual review of her CTA style factors (speed, size, co-movement).

worldview_premises.premise: Return dispersion among trend managers is structural and always underestimated, because parameterisation (horizon) makes return paths idiosyncratic despite high correlation.
Crowded positioning in 2024 was rewarded, so using a crowding measure to cut risk would have hurt.

steps.why: Expectations swung, so no persistent rate or FX trend

steps.from: Only equities (and a few commodities) trended
steps.why: Short undulations around rate and political regime change whipsawed fast models
Dispersion explained mostly by speed, not co-movement

mechanism_chains.fails_when: A broad multi-sector trend year or a signal not explained by speed.

decision_process.practice: Annual review of CTA style factors (speed, size, correlation) to see which sleeve of trend worked.
decision_process.why: Gives a decomposition of the year's trend performance.

speakers.evidence_style: Factor-based performance attribution on a large manager universe.

current_views.view: Slow, big-market trend won 2024; trends in less correlated markets did better; fast signals were hurt by policy-expectation noise.
current_views.reasoning: Style-factor spreads and the macro backdrop.

speakers.name: Nick Baltas

worldview_premises.premise: A sudden V-shaped shock hurts the middle trend speeds: very slow ones stay through, very fast ones trade it, medium ones go short at the bottom and are caught on the rebound.
Do not refit models after one event; behaviour is known and refitting overfits.
Crowding cannot be timed, and commentators' blame of CTAs, vol targeting, risk parity and QIS is often not supported by data.
worldview_premises.support: Anecdotes about 2024; says he does not see the data supporting QIS concentration claims.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend managers' returns differ for speed, universe, purity of trend versus reversion/carry, and discretionary de-risking.

steps.to: medium-speed models short at the low
steps.why: They flip short as the market recovers and double down on the loss

steps.to: outperformance of long winners over losers

mechanism_chains.evidence: Own data on a momentum implementation.

decision_process.practice: Treat one event as insufficient reason to refit; keep models stable.
In multi-strat context hold trend alongside reversion, carry, vol selling.
decision_process.why: Diversification smoothed a mediocre trend year.

speakers.evidence_style: Empirical, manager data and anecdotes; sceptical about unsupported narratives.

current_views.view: Carry appetite more conservative after August 2024; vol selling less rewarded in H2.
Single-stock momentum extremely strong in 2024, not an obvious crowded unwind.

speakers.name: Andrew Beer
speakers.role: Trend replication manager (top-down replication, hedge fund background)

worldview_premises.premise: Trend beta can be obtained cheaply by replication; fee budget should therefore go to esoteric alpha managers.
worldview_premises.support: Industry structure reasoning; his own commodity-firm experience (power markets: mean reversion, information asymmetry, liquidity provision).

worldview_premises.premise: Small parameter or sector-weight differences produce big and persistent dispersion; a simple top-down replication is more stable and adaptive.
worldview_premises.support: His 2015 survey of bank models and own build attempts.

worldview_premises.premise: Equity stock selection has become more efficient; AI will amplify biases in poor data.
worldview_premises.support: Career anecdotes (1990s vs now; hospital AI story).

worldview_premises.premise: Human beings are bad market timers; trend models are good at it.

steps.why: Fresh data points mixed with old regime

mechanism_chains.fails_when: Persistent trend reversal where slow de-risking loses.

decision_process.practice: Simple top-down replication rather than a bespoke trend model.

current_views.view: Simple models worked better in 2024 as major markets were stable; trend dispersion is normal not elevated.

worldview_premises.premise: Less liquid futures do not trend more; apparent evidence is a short-history artefact.
worldview_premises.support: Own review; histories coincide with strong trend periods; crypto shows the reverse.

worldview_premises.premise: Mean reversion is slow market making and so suits wide-spread illiquid markets.
The benefit of alternative markets is diversification.
AI has no serious use in his trading.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why illiquid markets look more trending

steps.to: history falls in good trend years

mechanism_chains.fails_when: A common-window study shows a significant effect.

current_views.view: No statistically significant liquidity effect in futures trend.

worldview_premises.premise: Efficiency is a joint hypothesis; outside equities there is no good valuation anchor, which is why trend following works (price is the valuation).
Machine learning is only marginally better or worse than simple trend benchmarks.
Manager dispersion largely disappears when managers are classified by style, timing and markets.

steps.to: assumed parallel shift down in curve
macro trend differs from market trend

decision_process.practice: Benchmark new models against simple existing ones.

current_views.view: Fed cut in Sept 2024 was followed by higher long yields, his biggest mistake.

worldview_premises.premise: Young markets trend more; maturity brings noise and mean reversion (Perry Kaufman).
A 2020 monetary regime shift produced idiosyncratic outlier trends; alternative markets diversify.
worldview_premises.support: 2024 moves in cocoa, coffee, OJ, bitcoin, yen crosses.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend manager return dispersion was very wide, and SG Trend Index is not representative.

decision_process.practice: Be very diversified to capture alternative markets.

current_views.view: Decoupling in financial markets is producing outlier trends.

positions.speaker: Andrew Beer
positions.position: Open question; uses to allocate alpha.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Several claims are unattributed in captions (panelist views on the vol specialist's segment, mistake discussion, local maximum).
Claim that 'trend following is never wrong' is a rhetorical point, ignores allocator timing errors raised right after.
Inconsistent attribution between Jim/Cem for the vol claims.
Quant statements (44% momentum, 12%/-10% speed factors) have no source data.
Duplicated claims on QIS and Dunne tension.

forward_looking_inputs: Speed of trend signals, equity-market trend persistence, index vol supply (structured products, income ETFs), dealer positioning, vol compression into January, Fed expectations vs long yields; horizons of months.
reader_inferences: The panel mostly explains past performance; few forward-testable signals apart from vol compression through January.
Speed vs state of macro (stable vs shock) is the main lever and is not forecastable ex ante.
